exhaustive.label: Length: exhaustive
exhaustive.sub: Cover everything that could possibly be relevant. Leave nothing out.

missed.label: Audience: someone who missed the whole semester
missed.sub: Assume they know nothing. Define every term before using it.

dense.label: Format: dense paragraphs
dense.sub: No headings. No bullets. Flowing prose, start to finish.

safe.label: Length: short and safe
safe.sub: Keep it brief. Don't risk being wrong about the details.

listicle.label: Format: numbered listicle
listicle.sub: Everything as a numbered list. Ten items. Equal weight to each.

peer.label: Audience: an expert peer
peer.sub: Assume deep familiarity. Skip the basics, get to the interesting part.

coach.label: Tone: encouraging coach
coach.sub: Lead with affirmation. Soften every critique. Protect motivation.

hedge.label: Coverage: hedge every claim
hedge.sub: Present all sides. Avoid committing to one recommendation.

scenarios.title: Help me get ready for my test
scenarios.base: Help me get ready for my test.

levers.context: I'm a sophomore in Mr. Dalton's Biology I class. The test is Friday and it covers cell structure, osmosis and diffusion, and the stages of mitosis. I've got about two hours to study tonight, and I bombed the last quiz on the mitosis stages — I keep mixing up metaphase and anaphase.
levers.success: Give me a one-page study guide I can print: a short section for each of the three topics, the 8–10 terms I'm most likely to be asked to define, and five practice questions with the answers at the bottom. No fluff — I should be able to read the whole thing in ten minutes.
levers.keywords: Focus on where people actually lose points: hypertonic vs. hypotonic direction of water flow, passive vs. active transport, and chromosome behavior at each phase. Use retrieval practice rather than a summary, and give me a discriminating cue for the pairs I confuse.

levers.context: I'm a 7th grader and my class is building popsicle-stick bridges for a competition Friday. Mine held about four pounds and then the middle snapped downward. I want to understand why it broke there so I can fix the design instead of just gluing on more sticks.
levers.success: Explain it in under 300 words, then give me three specific changes to try on my popsicle-stick bridge, in the order I should try them. Include one simple analogy I can repeat to my group.
levers.keywords: Explain it in terms of the load path, tension and compression members, bending moment, and where the neutral axis sits in my deck.

scenarios.title: Write an email to my boss
scenarios.base: Write an email to my boss.

levers.context: I'm a part-time shift lead at a grocery store. I need to ask my manager Renee for next Thursday and Friday off for my sister's wedding, three weeks out. I already asked Marcus and he'll cover Thursday; Friday is still open. I've never called out before and Renee is short-staffed right now.
levers.success: Under 120 words including the subject line. Plain and professional, not stiff. Make the ask in the first two sentences, say what I've already solved, and end with one clear question she can answer yes or no.
levers.keywords: Lead with the ask — BLUF — and frame it as a scheduling request with coverage already arranged. One call to action, no buried asks, and don't undercut it with hedging language.

scenarios.title: Here's my essay. Is it any good?
scenarios.base: Here's my essay. Is it any good?

levers.context: It's the argumentative essay for 11th grade English — the prompt was whether schools should start later. The rubric is 40% argument, 30% evidence, 20% organization, 10% conventions. My last one got marked down for "summarizing your sources instead of using them." The revision is due Monday.
levers.success: Don't rewrite it for me. Give me the three highest-leverage fixes in priority order, each one naming the sentence in my draft it applies to and what to do instead. Under 400 words. Be blunt — I'd rather hear it from you than from the grade.
levers.keywords: Check whether each body paragraph has a claim with a warrant connecting the evidence to my thesis, whether I'm signposting between paragraphs, and whether I'm dropping quotes without analysis.
